en: So how do we derive space complexity then?
It's relatively straightforward. When we
analyze our algorithm and we wanna judge the
space complexity, we have to find places,
lines of code in our algorithm where values
are stored permanently in memory. Now with
permanently, and that's why I put it between
quotes, I don't mean that it's there
forever. I just mean that, for example, if
you have a loop or a recursive function, it
survives that loop iteration or that
recursive step. So if you have a loop that
runs 3 times, that has 3 iterations, you
would create a new value with every
iteration and the value from the last
iteration would also still be used so that
you add one new value with every iteration.
That's what I mean with permanently. It's
not getting cleared up after a loop
iteration. It really is important for the
the entire runtime of your algorithm. As
long as your algorithm function runs, data
is used. If that's the case, then I refer to
such data as permanent data. Of course, it
will typically be cleared up once your
algorithm is done, but I'm really just
talking about the data management inside of
the running algorithm.
So we wanna look out for values that survive
multiple loop iterations or multiple
recursive steps. Steps in our algorithm,
and then we simply count how often such
permanently stored values are being created.
So how many such permanently stored values
we have in our algorithm.
And that then allows us to determine how
that number of permanently stored values
depends on n,
and this ultimately allows us to derive a
Big O notation. And yes, we also use the Big
O notation for space complexity. And there
we also can have a linear
or quadratic or exponential or logarithmic,
all kinds of space complexities in theory.
Because of course we could have an algorithm
where we, for example, create a new object
with every iteration in a loop
and we loop through
all numbers up to n and we keep the created
objects around after every iteration,
then we would have linear space complexity
because we would create more and more
objects and keep those objects around with a
growing n.
Of course, we'll see some real examples in
